I.	War is as old as humanity. Long before it became a matter of law or strategy, it was written into
our myths and instincts: the urge to dominate, the struggle for survival, the fall from paradise into
conflict. As the author Robert Ardrey once observed, we are not only animals; we are armed ones.
In modern times, the reality of war has become impossible to ignore. The photographs of
Hiroshima’s ruins, the televised images from the Vietnam War, the viral pictures from the Bucha
massacre in Ukraine and the latest livestreamed bombardments of Gaza all make clear what
earlier generations could more easily conceal or forget. War is not only the threat of violence. It is
the collapse of moral and political order: a moment when the rules of coexistence fall apart, laws
twist into something else, and human life loses its value, or takes on a new one. Yet even in such
devastation, responsibility does not disappear. To inherit war is to inherit the responsibility to
restrain it. In democracies, that burden is said to be shared — rooted in consent, exercised through
representation. And still, while war may be as old as humanity, democracy is not, and that
difference reshapes the questions citizens must ask.
What happens when the gravest of political acts — the decision to kill — is taken without the
citizens’ assent? That is the paradox of what I call the silent mandate: leaders treat the people’s
silence, which is structurally imposed, as if it were consent, turning absence into acquiescence. It
is the point where democracy keeps its name but loses its meaning. If conflict is the most serious
act a political community can undertake, shouldn’t it face a higher bar than ordinary political
decisions in a democratic state? And even if a conflict seems to meet the conditions of a ‘just war’ —
if such a thing exists — it may still be illegitimate if those in whose name it is fought were never
asked.

and money carries its own moral weight. The decision is made not on the battlefield but within
institutions that claim to speak for the people while avoiding their voice. Some doctrines allow for
war in so-called ‘supreme emergencies’. But can such reasoning ever suffice in a democracy, where
legitimacy should flow from the will of the people? Such silence is dangerous. It binds us, citizens,
to the consequences of war while denying us any role in deciding whether it should be waged.

has been done but in order that wrong may not be done.” www.lawpreptutorial.com

Tl. Japan, by giving up ideas of military supremacy, has reached a much more worthwhile objective—
economic supremacy.
In December 1941, during the Second World War, the U.S.A.’s top naval base, Pearl Harbour, on
the Pacific island of Hawaii, was attacked without prior warning by the Japanese. So severe was
the bombardment that, of the hundred odd naval vessels anchored there, only a handful survived.
This had the immediate effect of bringing America into the war as one of the Allied Powers. Up till
that point, the U.S.A. had had no direct involvement in hostilities save as a supplier of armaments
to the enemies of Japan. The Japanese attack had been uncalled-for and ill-considered, but they
did not realize the magnitude of their error until 1945, when America finally took its revenge by
dropping the first ever atom bombs on two of Japan’s major industrial centres, Hiroshima and
Nagasaki, thus annihilating Japan as a military power. The Americans then kept a tight military
and political hold over Japan. But the latter country, astonishingly, recuperated from the horror of
large-scale atomic devastation, and proceeded to adapt itself to an entirely new set of
circumstances. Before the Second World War, it had relied on the power of weapons. But after
witnessing the destruction they caused, it relinquished their use and set about reconstructing the
country along entirely peaceful lines.
Having once adopted this course, the Japanese showed great versatility, resilience and assiduity
and their success has been such that Japan is now considered the second greatest industrial power
in the entire world today. Its trade surplus is 37 billion dollars, more even than that of the U.S.A.
In the field of industry the victors have been defeated by the vanquished. Simply by accepting the
fact that aggression could not pay dividends and then channelizing its potential within the field of
industry, Japan has managed quite miraculously to supersede all the other nations of the world.
The Americans are greatly upset at this state of affairs and refer to the present ‘invasion’ of
Japanese goods as an Economic Pearl Harbour. A book recently published in America, under the
title of “Japan-Number One”, has become a best-seller. It clearly shows that Japan has far outrun
the U.S.A. in business and will soon supersede Britain. As far as foreign exchange is concerned,
Japan is the wealthiest country in the world, its foreign exchange reserves totalling 74 billion
dollars in 1984. [Economy; Word Count: 404]

questions.stimulus:
IV.	Our memories don’t all carry the same weight. Some moments settle into place without effort,
while others slip away almost immediately, leaving only the faintest trace behind. But what
pushes one experience toward long-term storage while another disappears? Is it the moment itself,
or the system deciding its fate?
A new study in Nature suggests the answer comes down to experience and timing. By examining
the hippocampus, thalamus, and cortex, researchers found that memories don’t become long-
lasting in a single step. Instead, they’re shaped by a cascade of molecular “timers” that activate
one after another, gradually determining which impressions consolidate into long-term memory.
This is a key revelation because it explains how we adjust the durability of memories. What we
choose to remember is a continuously evolving process rather than a one-time flipping of a switch.
For much of modern neuroscience, memory seemed straightforward. The hippocampus managed
short-term storage; with enough repetition or relevance, memories were thought to move into the
cortex and remain there. Existing models of memory in the brain involve transistor-like memory
molecules that act as on/off switches.

But that view couldn’t explain why some long-term memories fade quickly while others persist for
decades. In 2023, her lab identified a missing piece: a thalamic pathway that filters which
memories move toward long-term storage and routes them to the cortex. That raised a larger
question — once a memory leaves the hippocampus, what determines whether it sticks?
To track how memories mature, the researchers used a virtual-reality setup that let mice revisit
certain environments more often than others. This repetition created measurable differences in
how strongly each context was stored. The team then used a CRISPR-based approach to switch off
specific genes in the thalamus and cortex to test which molecular programs determine how long a
memory lasts. Their results revealed a stepwise sequence rather than a single mechanism.
Camtal, active early in the thalamus, stabilized new memories during their most vulnerable
stage. Tcf4, also in the thalamus, strengthened connections to the cortex as memories matured.
Ashll, a later-acting regulator in the cortex, triggered chromatin remodeling that helped convert a
fragile trace into something more durable. Disrupting any part of this sequence didn’t erase
memories — it simply caused them to fade sooner. Unless you promote memories onto these
timers, we believe you're primed to forget it quickly.

VII. The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has directed Indian smartphone companies,
including manufacturers and importers, to pre-install the state-developed cybersecurity
application called Sanchar Saathi. The DoT directive, issued on November 28 under the
Telecommunication Cybersecurity Amendment Rules, 2025, sparked criticism over privacy and
surveillance issues. The diktat effectively meant that users had no say in whether they wanted to
use the app, and no option to remove it if their phone came preinstalled with it. For this to work in
practice, the app will almost certainly need system level or root level access, similar to carrier or
OEM system apps, so that it cannot be disabled. That design choice erodes the protections that
normally prevent one app from peering into the data of others, and turns Sanchar Saathi into a
permanent, non-consensual point of access sitting inside the operating system of every Indian
smartphone user. This is the first time the government has issued a directive mandating the
installation of a state-backed application on phones. While such a move would be unusual in most
Western democracies, it is not entirely without precedent. Besides, when the Telecommunications
Act was being finalised in 2023, several concerns were raised that the law might be broad and
cover online platforms as well. While the government had then said that no such overlaps would
happen, the telecom cybersecurity rules, which draw their powers from the Telecom Act, are now
being used to issue directions to tech companies.
[Sanchar Saathi App Controversy; Word Count: 241]

X.	Under Section 2(a) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a proposal is made when one person signifies
to another his willingness to do or abstain from doing something with a view to obtaining the
other’s assent. A proposal must be definite, specific, communicated, and made with the intention of
acceptance. Once accepted, it becomes a promise and creates binding obligations; if not accepted,
no contract arises.
An invitation to offer is a preliminary communication inviting negotiations and does not create
legal obligations. Advertisements, price lists, catalogues, shop displays, and invitations to tender
are classic examples. Courts have consistently held that such communications are not offers but
invitations to treat, as seen in Pharmaceutical Products of India Ltd. v. Gwalior Chemical Works
Ltd., Fisher v. Bell, Mohanlal v. Kashiram, Harvela Investments Ltd. v. Royal Trust Co. of
Canada, and Harvey v. Facey.
Intention to create a legal relationship is an essential element of a valid contract. While
commercial agreements generally presume such intention, social or domestic arrangements do not.
In Balfour v. Balfour, a domestic promise lacked legal intention, whereas in Merritt v. Merritt, a
written agreement between separated spouses showed clear intent and consideration, making it
enforceable.
Communication of offer is necessary. In Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt, the court reiterated that
acceptance can be by performance of the required act, provided the offer is known.
Offers may be cross offers (Tinn v. Hoffman), counter-offers (Hyde v. Wrench), specific or general
(Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.). Offers may also be standing, open, or continuing, as explained
in Bengal Coal Co. v. Homee Wadia & Co. and Rajendra Kumar v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
These principles collectively govern proposal and acceptance under contract law. [Indian Contract
Act- Proposal; Word Count: 284]

questions.stimulus:
XI.	General defences in tort law are legal principles that allow a defendant to escape liability for a
tortious act. These defences operate to protect the defendant’s legal rights where liability would
otherwise arise. While the plaintiff bears the burden of proving the tort, the defendant may avoid
liability by successfully establishing a recognised defence. The purpose of these defences is to
maintain a fair balance between the rights of the plaintiff and the defendant and to ensure that
liability is not imposed where the defendant’s conduct was justified or beyond their control.
The application of general defences depends entirely on the facts and circumstances of each case. A
defendant must clearly show that their actions fall within the scope of a particular defence. The
major general defences include volenti non fit injuria, plaintiff the wrongdoer, inevitable accident,
act of God, private defence, mistake, necessity, and statutory authority.
Volenti non fit injuria is based on consent, meaning that a person who knowingly and voluntarily
assumes a risk cannot later complain of injury arising from that risk. The defence of volenti non fit
injuria does not apply in rescue situations. The defence of plaintiff the wrongdoer, expressed in the
maxim ex turpi causa non oritur actio, bars a claim where the plaintiff's own wrongful conduct
substantially contributed to the harm. Inevitable accident applies where harm occurs despite all
reasonable care and was not foreseeable, whereas act of God refers to harm caused solely by
natural forces beyond human control.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Private defence justifies reasonable force used to protect person or property, but excessive or
unjustified force negates the defence. Mistake, even if made in good faith, is generally not a
defence in tort. Necessity allows limited interference with rights to prevent greater harm but is
narrowly applied. Statutory authority protects acts expressly or impliedly authorised by law,
though negligence in execution may still attract liability. [General Defences under Tort Law; Word
Count: 312]

questions.stimulus:
XII. Indian law classifies a father’s property into two categories: ancestral property and self-acquired
property. The rights of sons and daughters vary significantly depending on this classification.
Ancestral property is joint family property inherited through four generations of male lineage and
remains undivided. Rights in such property arise by birth and not by succession after death.
A major change was introduced by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which conferred
equal coparcenary rights on daughters, placing them at par with sons. Daughters became
coparceners by birth with equal rights and liabilities, irrespective of marital status. Courts have
clarified that daughters born before 2005 or whose fathers died before the amendment can also
claim rights, provided no valid partition occurred before 20 December 2004. Married daughters
retain full coparcenary rights in ancestral property and can demand partition.
Self-acquired property refers to property acquired by the father through his own efforts or
earnings. During the father’s lifetime, sons and daughters have no rights in such property, and the
father has absolute freedom to transfer it. Rights arise only after the father’s death. If a valid will
exists, property devolves according to the will. In the absence of a will, sons and daughters inherit
equally as Class I heirs under the Hindu Succession Act.

Partition in ancestral property converts joint ownership into individual ownership, after which
each share becomes self-acquired. Adopted children enjoy the same rights as biological children.
Children born from void or voidable marriages can inherit self-acquired property but do not
automatically acquire coparcenary rights. Different personal laws apply to Muslims, Christians,
and Parsis. A father may gift property during his lifetime, subject to statutory requirements.
[Ancestral Property under Family Law; Word Count: 274]

ancestral-property-and-inherited-property/

questions.stimulus:
XIII. Article 32 occupies a central position in the Indian constitutional framework. During the
Constituent Assembly debates, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described it as the very heart and soul of the
Constitution, stressing that Fundamental Rights are meaningless without effective remedies.
Introduced against the backdrop of colonial denial of civil liberties, Article 32 empowers citizens to
directly approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of their Fundamental Rights.
Article 32 comprises four clauses. It grants individuals the right to move the Supreme Court for
enforcement of Fundamental Rights, empowers the Court to issue writs such as habeas corpus,
mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto, allows Parliament to confer similar powers
on other courts, and protects this right from suspension except as constitutionally permitted
during emergencies. It is a remedial fundamental right and has been recognised as part of the
basic structure of the Constitution, notably in Minerva Mills v. Union of India.
A unique feature of Article 32 is direct access to the Supreme Court without exhausting
alternative remedies. Through its writ jurisdiction, the Court protects personal liberty, ensures
performance of public duties, restrains jurisdictional excesses, quashes illegal orders, and prevents
unlawful occupation of public offices. However, writ jurisdiction is discretionary and subject to
limitations such as locus standi, availability of alternative remedies, delay, and res judicata.
Article 32 applies only to Fundamental Rights and generally not to private disputes.
The scope of Article 32 expanded through Public Interest Litigation, allowing public-spirited
individuals to approach the Court on behalf of marginalised groups, as recognised in S.P. Gupta v.
Union of India. Compared to Article 226, Article 32 is narrower in scope but stronger as a
guaranteed right. Despite suspension of Article 32 during emergencies under Article 359, core
rights under Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable. Overall, Article 32 serves as a dynamic
instrument of constitutional justice and judicial review. [Article 32 under Indian Constitutional
Framework; Word Count: 307]

questions.stimulus:
XIV. Patent revocation refers to the cancellation of rights granted to a patent holder, after which the
patent is treated as if it never existed. Revocation proceedings may be initiated by any person
interested, the Central Government, or by way of a counterclaim in an infringement suit before
the High Court. The objective of revocation is to prevent unjust monopolies and ensure that only
valid inventions enjoy protection.
Section 64 of the Patents Act, 1970 provides exhaustive grounds for revocation. A patent may be
revoked if the invention was already claimed in an earlier Indian patent, granted to an unentitled
person, or wrongfully obtained from the true inventor. Revocation is also possible where the
subject matter is not an “invention”, lacks novelty or inventive step, was secretly used in India
prior to filing, or is not useful. Insufficient disclosure, failure to disclose the best method, unclear
claims, false suggestions, or misrepresentation also render a patent vulnerable to revocation.
Patents covering non-patentable subject matter under Sections 3 and 4, failure to disclose the
source of biological material, anticipation by traditional knowledge, violation of Section 8 (non-

disclosure of foreign filings), breach of secrecy directions, or fraudulent amendments can equally
lead to revocation.
Apart from Section 64, post-grant opposition under Section 25(2) allows challenges within one year
of grant. Section 65 enables revocation of patents relating to atomic energy, while Section 66
empowers the Government to revoke patents prejudicial to public interest. Section 85 permits
revocation for non-working of patents after grant of a compulsory licence.
Patent revocation is crucial to balance innovation with public interest. It prevents wrongful
monopolies, protects traditional knowledge, ensures affordability and access, and maintains the
integrity of India’s patent system.
[Patent revocation; Word Count: 281]

patent is treated as if it never existed. Revocation proceedings may be initiated by any person
interested, the Central Government, or by way of a counterclaim in an infringement suit before
the High Court. The objective of revocation is to prevent unjust monopolies and ensure that only
valid inventions enjoy protection.
Section 64 of the Patents Act, 1970 provides exhaustive grounds for revocation. A patent may be
revoked if the invention was already claimed in an earlier Indian patent, granted to an unentitled
person, or wrongfully obtained from the true inventor. Revocation is also possible where the
subject matter is not an “invention”, lacks novelty or inventive step, was secretly used in India
prior to filing, or is not useful. Insufficient disclosure, failure to disclose the best method, unclear
claims, false suggestions, or misrepresentation also render a patent vulnerable to revocation.
Patents covering non-patentable subject matter under Sections 3 and 4, failure to disclose the
source of biological material, anticipation by traditional knowledge, violation of Section 8 (non-

disclosure of foreign filings), breach of secrecy directions, or fraudulent amendments can equally
lead to revocation.
Apart from Section 64, post-grant opposition under Section 25(2) allows challenges within one year
of grant. Section 65 enables revocation of patents relating to atomic energy, while Section 66
empowers the Government to revoke patents prejudicial to public interest. Section 85 permits
revocation for non-working of patents after grant of a compulsory licence.
Patent revocation is crucial to balance innovation with public interest. It prevents wrongful
monopolies, protects traditional knowledge, ensures affordability and access, and maintains the
integrity of India’s patent system.
[Patent revocation; Word Count: 281]

that is available only for a limited period after grant. The patentee argues that this route is time-

time-limited post-grant route.

without any limitation period.

grant.

options.label: c
options.text:
The challenger is correct because any delay is cured if the patent is alleged to harm public
interest and affordability.

options.label: d

The patentee is correct only if it proves the challenger is not a “person interested” and lacks
standing to object.

A patentee obtains a patent for a mechanical device but describes the invention in vague terms
and does not disclose the best method of performing it. A competitor argues that the disclosure is
insufficient and misleading, making it impossible for a skilled person to work the invention
properly. The patentee responds that once the patent is granted, disclosure defects cannot be used

Which option is most accurate?

The competitor is correct because insufficient disclosure and failure to disclose the best method
render a patent vulnerable to revocation.

options.label: b

The patentee is correct because disclosure issues can be raised only at filing, not after the
patent is granted.

options.label: c
options.text:
The competitor is correct only if it also proves the invention lacks novelty, since disclosure
defects alone cannot matter in patent revocation.

options.label: d
options.text:
The patentee is correct because unclear claims can be corrected later, so they can never
support cancellation.

A patent is granted for a “method of improving mango sweetness” using a process that farmers in
a region claim has been practiced for decades and is documented in local traditional knowledge
records. A public organisation files a challenge stating the claimed method is already known
through traditional knowledge and should not enjoy exclusive protection. The patentee argues that
because the invention is commercially useful, it cannot be cancelled.
Which is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
The patentee is correct because commercial usefulness alone ensures the patent remains valid
despite prior traditional knowledge.

options.label: b

The challenger is correct because patents anticipated by traditional knowledge can be revoked
even if the product is useful.

options.label: c
options.text:
The patentee is correct because traditional practices are irrelevant unless they were published
in an international journal.

options.label: d
options.text:
The challenger is correct only if it proves the patentee copied the method with dishonest intent
and not otherwise.

questions.stimulus:
XV. ‘Transferable property refers to property that can be legally transferred from one person to another
through recognised modes such as sale, gift, lease, mortgage or exchange. Section 6 of the Transfer
of Property Act, 1882 lays down the general rule that property of any kind may be transferred,
subject to statutory restrictions. Transferable property includes immovable property like land and
buildings, movable assets such as vehicles and machinery, intellectual property like patents and
copyrights, and financial instruments such as shares and securities.
Non-transferable property consists of interests that cannot be legally transferred due to their
personal, contingent or restricted nature. Section 6 enumerates specific exceptions to
transferability. Spes succession is, or the mere chance of an heir apparent inheriting property, is
non-transferable under Section 6(a), as affirmed in Official Assignee, Madras v. Sampath Naidu.
Similarly, the right of re-entry, easements apart from the dominant heritage, and interests
restricted to personal enjoyment cannot be transferred. Rights such as future maintenance, a mere
right to sue, public offices, salaries attached to public offices, and pensions are expressly non-
transferable.
Section 6 also prohibits transfers opposed to the nature of the interest, transfers for unlawful
objects or consideration, and transfers to legally disqualified persons. Statutory prohibitions
further restrict transfer of certain tenancy or occupancy rights, as recognised in Shanti Prasad v.
Bachchi Devi. Courts have consistently held that these restrictions preserve the purpose, dignity
and legal character of such interests. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The distinction between transferable and non-transferable property is crucial. Transferable
property offers flexibility, marketability and economic value, while non-transferable property is
protected due to its personal, public, religious or statutory character. Section 6 thus balances
freedom of transfer with legal, moral and public policy considerations, ensuring orderly and lawful
transfer of property rights. [Transferable and Non-Transferable Property; Word Count: 289]

transferable-property/
questions.stem:
Ramesh executes a written gift deed transferring his farmhouse to his friend Vinay. Vinay argues
that any property can be transferred in law if the parties agree and the document is registered.
Ramesh’s brother objects, saying some transfers are barred by law even if both parties consent.
The dispute is only about whether the law allows transfer in general, not about stamp duty or
registration.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
Any property of any kind may be transferred, but only subject to statutory restrictions
recognised by law.

options.label: b
options.text:
No property can ever be transferred unless a court first grants permission for that specific
transfer.

options.label: c
options.text:
Any property becomes transferable if it is registered, because registration cures all legal
restrictions.

options.label: d
options.text:
Property can be transferred only if it is immovable; movable and intangible rights are never
transferable.

questions.stem:
Shalini’s father is alive but elderly. Shalini’s cousin, who expects to inherit as an heir apparent,
signs an agreement “selling” his expected future share in the father’s property to a financier for
immediate cash. After the father later changes his plans, the financier sues Shalini’s cousin for
specific enforcement of the “sale.” The cousin argues that he sold only a chance, not an existing
property interest.
Which option is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
The financier will succeed because an heir apparent’s expected inheritance is treated as
valuable property that can be sold.

options.label: b
options.text:
The financier will succeed because future inheritance becomes transferable once money
consideration is paid.

options.label: c
options.text:
The cousin will succeed because the mere chance of an heir apparent inheriting property is
non-transferable.

options.label: d
options.text:
The cousin will succeed only if he proves the financier knew the father was likely to change his
plans later.

questions.stem:
Gita holds occupancy rights in agricultural land under a local tenancy statute that restricts
transfer without government permission. She “sells” these occupancy rights to a trader through a
simple agreement and takes full payment. Later, the trader sues for possession, claiming that
occupancy rights are like ordinary property and can always be sold. Gita argues that statutory
prohibitions restrict such transfers.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
The trader will succeed because once consideration is paid, even restricted tenancy or
occupancy rights become transferable.

options.label: b
options.text:
The trader will succeed because statutory restrictions apply only to ownership rights, not to
occupancy or tenancy rights.

options.label: c
options.text:
Gita will succeed only if she proves the trader acted dishonestly, otherwise the transfer must
be enforced.

options.label: d
options.text:
Gita will succeed because statutory prohibitions further restrict transfer of certain tenancy or
occupancy rights.

questions.stem:
A municipal employee assigns his monthly government pension to a private lender to secure a
loan, promising that the lender can directly collect the pension from his bank account. Later, the
employee defaults and the lender sues, arguing the assignment was voluntary and commercially
necessary. The employee argues that certain rights are protected from transfer regardless of
consent.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
The lender will succeed because any right becomes transferable if the owner voluntarily agrees
to assign it.

options.label: b
options.text:
The lender will succeed because pensions are treated like ordinary income and can be freely
transferred to repay debts.

options.label: c
options.text:
The employee will succeed because pensions are expressly non-transferable interests protected
by law.

options.label: d
options.text:
The employee will succeed only if he proves the lender used coercion; otherwise voluntary
transfer is always valid.

Farhan leases a small shop to Nitin for running a lawful pharmacy. Nitin then agrees to “transfer”
his lease rights to a person who is legally disqualified from holding such premises under local
rules, to hide that person’s involvement. Farhan objects, saying the transfer is barred because it is
being made to a disqualified person and for an unlawful arrangement. Nitin argues that any
transfer is valid if parties consent.
Which option is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
Nitin is correct because consent of the parties always overrides restrictions on the identity of
the transferee.

options.label: b
options.text:
Nitin is correct because lease rights are always transferable, regardless of unlawful object or
legal disqualification.

options.label: c
options.text:
Farhan is correct only if he proves the pharmacy business itself was illegal, otherwise the
transfer must stand.

options.label: d
options.text: Farhan is correct because Section 6 prohibits transfers to legally disqualified persons.

sustaining such creativity becomes harder. Women balancing long work hours with household
chores often lack the space to explore such avenues.

society groups, start-ups, and individuals are stepping in. This is where domestic workers and
other women in the unorganised sector are experimenting with art, craft, and design-empowering
themselves in the process. One such initiative is The Sunflower Ladies. Their social media
showcases sunflower-embroidered tote bags, crocheted planters in radiant hues of yellow, green,
orange, and brown, and even Van Gogh-inspired headbands drawn from the artist’s iconic
sunflower paintings. Maya and Kausilya, both domestic workers in South Delhi, relentlessly
crochet sunflower patterns on tote bags after their daily work hours. Over time, this small activity
has blossomed into a vibrant creative enterprise.
For women, these gatherings are not just about economic opportunities but also about reclaiming
leisure time —spaces where they get together to laugh, socialise, and express themselves,
especially domestic workers who rarely get the chance to pursue creative hobbies. Banagloo, in
fact, has already tied up with several other civil society organisations working with residents of
shelter homes and the differently abled, as well as domestic workers. This model of community-led
craft-making demonstrates how cultural and social capital can be generated simultaneously.

coming together itself builds confidence, camaraderie, and recognition.

and identity. These stories highlight the resilience of women in the face of urban poverty. Given
the right opportunities, they harness them with creativity and determination. What is needed now
is greater support from government schemes, CSR programmes, and individuals to scale such
initiatives, making invisible talents visible, and ensuring that art and livelihood walk hand in
hand. [Lifestyle; Word Count: 414]

XVIII. At the start of the year, Earth will quietly reach a milestone in its orbit around the sun. Known as
perihelion, this is the moment when our planet is closer to the sun than at any other point in the
year.
In 2026, Earth's perihelion occurs on January 3 at 12:15 p.m. EST or 17:15 UTC. This
astronomical event occurs about two weeks after the December solstice. The exact timing shifts
slightly from year to year because the Gregorian calendar doesn't perfectly line up with Earth's
orbit. However, leap years account for some of that discrepancy. It might sound counterintuitive to
some that Earth is closest to the sun right now—after all, January is winter across much of the
Northern Hemisphere. But Earth's axial tilt is actually the dominant driver of seasons, not Earth's
distance from the sun. Perihelion does influence the Earth, from how fast our planet moves
through space to how long each season lasts. However, it doesn’t mean that the sun will appear
substantially larger in the sky.

While you might expect Earth's path around the sun to be a perfect circle, it's actually an ellipse,
with the sun positioned just slightly off-center. As a result, the distance between Earth and the
sun changes continuously over the course of a year. At its simplest, perihelion is the point in the
orbit of a planet, comet, or other astronomical body where it is closest to the sun. Its counterpart is
aphelion, or a celestial body's farthest distance from the sun.
The change in Earth’s distance from the sun is fairly minimal, however, and perihelion isn't
something you'd notice with the naked eye. At perihelion, Earth is about 91.4 million miles from
the sun compared to roughly 94.5 million miles at aphelion in July. The Earth's orbit is also
constantly changing from interactions with the other planets in the solar system, especially the
Moon and Jupiter, so the time of perihelion can shift by a few hours. While Earth's changing
distance from the sun does affect our climate, perihelion does not have a drastic impact on our
seasons. www. lawpreptutorial.com
